summary:
Bihār has no state-specific transgender legislation of its own. A trans visitor to the state stands directly under India's national framework, and no source material indicates a deviation in Bihār material enough to score separately from the national position.

That national framework was substantially rewritten in March 2026. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in both houses, amending the 2019 Act, and the measure awaits presidential assent. It removes the right to self-identification recognised by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment declaring transgender people a third gender, and limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme entirely. The amendment also mandates medical certification as the basis for identity recognition on documents.

Rights organisations describe the change as a major setback that strips thousands of people of rights and increases their exposure to harm. Activists including Akkai Padmashali have characterised the amendment as criminalising and as an attack on the right to exist. The Government of India presents the amendment as widening access to welfare schemes and strengthening protection against trafficking; critics respond that it excludes a large share of transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India's transgender population is estimated at two million.

The entry and stay baseline for LGBT+ visitors remains mixed on other axes. The Supreme Court decriminalised same-sex sexual acts in 2018, and statutory anti-discrimination protection on grounds including sex has been interpreted to encompass gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available anywhere in India, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units for limited purposes.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded transgender people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code. The absence of that protection applies in Bihār on the same terms as elsewhere in the country.

Document and checkpoint friction is documented at several points of entry. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a transgender applicant to sit a medical examination as part of the process; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The high courts remain the strongest protection machinery available. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh after police harassment of a same-sex couple, issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and to education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people in India, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor to Bihār, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone. Recognition was narrowed nationally in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abusive encounters at railway stations, airports and passport offices were documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of transgender and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The 2026 amendment has been defended on welfare grounds rather than on identity grounds. The government's stated rationale is that the new recognition criteria make cash and scheme benefits easier to deliver to the groups historically associated with transgender status in India, including hijra and kinner communities, and that trafficking protection follows from a narrower, verifiable category.

Passage of the bill drew protests from opposition parties and from LGBTQ organisations across India, who say the change cuts off access to education, healthcare and formal employment for people whose identity is not expressed through the traditional categories. Reports of uneven recognition and continuing discrimination in those three sectors form part of the national background that applies in Bihār.

The recognition debate sits against a longer constitutional history: the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that recognised transgender people as a third gender with full fundamental rights is the baseline the amendment narrows, and the 2018 decriminalisation of same-sex conduct is the other pillar of the current legal position. Neither has been withdrawn, but the practical weight of the 2014 recognition has been reduced.

The security and checkpoint pattern identified in 2024 spans multiple agencies rather than a single institution: railway protection forces at stations, central industrial security force personnel at airports, and passport authorities at consulates and passport offices. The documented cases include physical contact, humiliating treatment in custody, and demands for medical verification.

Comparatively, India's position now rests on court-made protection rather than on self-declaration in statute. The Madras High Court guidelines of 2021, the Allahabad High Court relief of February 2026, and the family-unit acknowledgments by courts all indicate that remedies run through litigation rather than through administrative recognition.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bihār who hold identity documents under the 2019 framework face a change of basis. The 2026 amendment makes medical certification the condition for identity recognition, so the route to a corrected or updated document runs through a certifying medical process rather than through a declaration.

Transgender residents outside the historically recognised socio-cultural groups have no route to legal recognition under the amended scheme, which affects access to welfare schemes, employment benefits and any process that depends on a recognised category.

The removal of the gender-identity-specific offences in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita applies to residents of Bihār as it does to residents of every other state. Transgender people reporting sexual violence therefore proceed under general offence provisions rather than under the targeted sections that existed under the Indian Penal Code.

Residents encountering police in Bihār are covered by the Madras High Court guidelines only insofar as those guidelines have been applied as persuasive authority or implemented by the state police. The source material does not describe Bihār's own police sensitisation measures.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source material does not confirm whether the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill has received presidential assent. Both houses passed it in March 2026, but assent was pending at the time of the reporting cited here, and the current legal status of the amendment is therefore unresolved.

No source in the inventory addresses enforcement practice specific to Bihār. The absence of Bihār-specific findings means the state assessment rests entirely on the national framework; it does not establish that enforcement in Bihār matches the national pattern in either direction.

The operational detail of the medical certification requirement is not specified in the sources. Which authorities certify, what procedure applies, and whether a visitor with foreign documents can obtain such certification are not sourced.

Whether Bihār operates a state transgender welfare board, a state-level implementation of the 2019 Act, or any state police guidance on transgender contacts is not covered by the inventory and remains unresolved.

The inventory contains no reporting on border or immigration screening practice specific to transgender travellers entering India, beyond the domestic checkpoint and passport cases cited. The risk assessment for entry therefore rests on those documented domestic encounters rather than on any sourced account of immigration procedure.
